newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ten years jail for "forced" Srebrenica executioner.
newsitem.headline: Ten years jail for "forced" Srebrenica executioner.

text.p: A U.N. warcrimes tribunal on Friday sentenced a Croat who confessed to taking part in the Bosnian Serb Army (BSA) massacre of over 1,200 unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica to 10 years in jail.

Drazen Erdemovic, 25, is the first person to be sentenced by the Hague-based U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia and the first sentenced by an international war crimes tribunal since the Nuremburg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
He pleaded guilty in May to being one of the BSA's execution squad that carried out the killings after the United Nations "safe haven" was captured by Serbs in July 1995.

Reading the verdict, presiding judge Claude Jorda of France said the three-judge panel had taken into account the accused's age, his low military rank, his remorse at the crimes committed and his "full and unconditional" cooperation with prosecutors.
Erdemovic sat impassively throughout the 45-minute reading and after the verdict shook hands and spoke briefly with his lawyer.

At pre-sentencing hearings earlier this month, the prosecution recommended Erdemovic be jailed for no longer than 10 years, recognising that he had confessed, shown remorse and provided valuable information about war crimes.
Erdemovic's defence had argued that the ex-soldier should be acquitted because he had been forced to take part in the summary execution of Moslems under threat of death.
The tribunal, set up by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, cannot impose the death penalty, but may hand down a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.
Erdemovic, a Croat who served in the BSA, was the first insider from the Bosnian Serb military to publicly testify about events at Srebrenica.
He was arrested in March by Belgrade authorities after telling French newspaper Le Figaro how he had personally killed 70 Moslems during the mass execution.

"His testimony exposed the lies of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders that the killings of civilians from Srebrenica was nothing but Moslem propaganda," prosecutor Mark Harmon said during pre-sentencing hearings on November 20.
In his guilty plea, Erdemovic said Moslem civilians were bussed to Branjevo farm at Pilica, near Zvornik some 70 kms north of Srebrenica, where they were shot in groups of 10 by his BSA unit.
He insisted that he had no choice but to take part in the five-hour killing spree as the officer in charge had threatened to kill him if he did not carry out the order.

Prosecutors admit that Erdemovic would have remained a "faceless, nameless executioner" and the tribunal might never have unveiled the Pilica massacre -- which it said was "amongst the largest crimes committed during the tragic conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina" -- if Erdemovic himself had not spoken out.

The young Croat also testified at public hearings in July against deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former military chief General Ratko Mladic, both of whom have been charged with genocide for the killings after the fall of Srebrenica. Both remain at large.
At the earlier hearings, Erdemovic spoke of his regret at the deaths on all sides of the war in Bosnia.
"I have lost many good friends of many nationalities...They were not in favour of war...they simply had no other choice. This war came and there was no way out and the same happened to me," he said.
Erdemovic is unlikely to serve his sentence at the tribunal's detention unit in the Hague, where he has been held since late-March.

States which have offered to enforce tribunal sentences are: Bosnia, Croatia, Iran, Finland, Norway and Pakistan. Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden would take take convicted war criminals, with reservations.
The accused has 30 days in which to appeal the sentence.
